title: The African church
hook: from an Ethiopian official on a desert road to packed churches across the continent, the map of Christianity has shifted south

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pentecostalism worldwide, a sawdust floor on Azusa Street and revivals breaking out in many places at once. Your line was the spirit on all flesh. Whose voice did you let finish? Day nine hundred seventy-six.

A chariot is rolling along the desert road that goes down from Jerusalem toward Gaza. In it sits a royal treasurer from the court of the queen of the Ethiopians, heading home after worshiping in Jerusalem. He has a scroll of Isaiah open on his knees, and he's reading out loud. A man named Philip runs up alongside and calls out, in the King James Bible: "Understandest thou what thou readest?" The official invites him up. Further on, they pass some water, and the official says: "See, here is water; what doth hinder me to be baptized?" Today, the African church, which starts earlier than some people expect.

That Ethiopian official goes home baptized, in the eighth chapter of Acts, and the Bible never mentions him again. But Africa doesn't leave the story. Egypt's Coptic Christians trace their church to Mark, the Gospel writer, by tradition. Some early Christian writers came from North Africa, Augustine among them. Ethiopia has its own ancient church, with its own scriptures in the old language Ge'ez and churches carved straight down into the rock. So when people call Christianity a Western religion that arrived in Africa with Europeans, the Bible itself and these old churches answer back. Then came a harder chapter. European missionaries arrived alongside colonial rule, and the two got tangled together; schools, hospitals and translated Bibles came with land taken and cultures dismissed. Historians of African Christianity also stress something easy to miss: much of the spreading was done by Africans themselves, catechists, evangelists, prophets and ordinary converts, often well beyond any missionary's reach. Some started churches of their own, African independent churches, praying in their own languages and music. Today the continent is full of church life: Anglicans in Nigeria and Uganda, Catholics in Congo, Orthodox in Ethiopia, Pentecostals in Ghana and Kenya, and many more. Some who study world Christianity say its center of gravity has moved south, away from Europe and North America. And the traffic now runs both ways: some African churches plant congregations in London, Houston and Berlin. Some readers see the treasurer on the desert road as an early sign of where the story was heading.

Here's the practice: travel the continent in prayer or in thought. Settle, and breathe. Start in the north, at a Coptic church in Cairo. Move south to a stone church in the Ethiopian highlands, then a cathedral in Kampala, a tin-roofed chapel in a village, a big Pentecostal gathering in Lagos. Then come home to any African congregation meeting in your own city. Stop at one. Listen for it: a choir, a drum, a language you may not know. If you pray, you can pray for that church and the people in it. If you don't, send them good will in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Ethiopian. The queen's treasurer who read Isaiah on the desert road and was baptized, an early sign some see of the African church to come.
Your line: the center has moved. Today, look for one Christian voice from Africa, a hymn, a sermon, a writer, and listen to it. Day nine hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: African churches range from the ancient Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo and Coptic Orthodox churches to Catholic, Anglican, Protestant, Pentecostal and African independent churches. Worship is commonly in local languages, with music, singing and dancing.

original.note: Greek: Ethiopian, the word Acts 8:27 uses for the treasurer of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians.

trapdoor: what you thought: Christianity came to Africa with European missionaries.
what it means: Africa is in the Book of Acts, has ancient churches, and is now a center of Christian life.
what a scholar hears: Aithiops in Acts 8, the queen called Candace, and a story some read as the faith heading south from the start.

notes: Claims rule: the index hook's statistic ('Africa now has more Christians than any other continent') is not stated; it is rendered as an attributed, non-numeric claim ('Some who study world Christianity say its center of gravity has moved south'). Confirm the Keeper is content with that.
The road 'down from Jerusalem toward Gaza' follows Acts 8:26; 'Further on' glosses 8:36.
Coptic tradition of Mark as founder is attributed ('by tradition'). Augustine (Hippo, in present-day Algeria) as a North African writer: confirm.
Ethiopian Orthodox scriptures in Ge'ez and rock-hewn churches (Lalibela): confirm.
'Historians of African Christianity also stress... much of the spreading was done by Africans themselves' is an attributed general claim; confirm.
The 'many more' list of churches by country is illustrative; confirm. 'Some African churches plant congregations in London, Houston and Berlin': confirm or generalize.
'Starts earlier than some people expect' is a soft general claim; soften if needed.
Original: Αἰθίοψ (Acts 8:27); in Greek usage it referred broadly to peoples south of Egypt (here the kingdom of Kush/Meroë); confirm the note.
Editor pass: cut the superlative 'great' early writers; varied a practice closing line repeated across nearby days; original note now says only what Acts 8:27 says, without the unsourced geography.

Editor pass 2: practice rewritten as a north-to-south journey because it repeated day 975's 'picture the people arriving, the music starting'; 'often tangled' softened; the closing 'turns out to be an early sign' and the trapdoor are now attributed to some readers; fork reveal 'at the first water' changed to follow Acts 8:36 ('a certain water').
